name: Ptolemaic Egypt
title: Social Hierarchy of Ptolemaic Egypt: From Pharaoh to Enslaved
period: 305–30 BCE (the 3rd century BCE, under the first four Ptolemies)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are hailed as basileus by the Greeks and as pharaoh by the Egyptians; in theory the whole economy of Egypt is yours to command, and the temples show you in the dress of the old kings.
tiers.kid: The king was a Greek from Macedonia who ruled Egypt as its pharaoh from the great city of Alexandria.
tiers.rise: The crown passed within the dynasty, usually to the king’s son, often first as co-ruler: Ptolemy I shared his rule with Ptolemy II in 285 BCE. Under Ptolemy IV royal favourites controlled the government, and in 205 BCE a priest, Horwennefer, proclaimed himself pharaoh in Upper Egypt.
tiers.why: The king was a Macedonian Greek.

tiers.name: The court and royal officials
tiers.term: strategos (governor of a nome), oikonomos (steward of a nome), komarches (village administrator)
tiers.you: You serve the king at Alexandria, or govern a nome as its strategos, managing its wealth for the crown; like nearly every holder of a high post, you are a Greek.
tiers.kid: Greek officials ran Egypt for the king, and they collected taxes from every province and village.
tiers.rise: Office came by the king’s appointment, and Greeks held nearly all of it; over time Egyptians who spoke Greek could rise further. Favour could also be lost: under Ptolemy IV a circle of royal favourites took control of the government.
tiers.why: Around the king stood a Greek court and a complex bureaucracy built to extract Egypt’s wealth for the crown.

tiers.name: Egyptian priests
tiers.you: You serve in an Egyptian temple that the Greek king has rebuilt and endowed; your synod hails him as Horus, while his officials tax the temple’s land.
tiers.kid: Egyptian priests looked after the temples, and the Greek kings built new temples to keep the priests on their side.
tiers.rise: Priestly office stayed in Egyptian hands. A priest could serve the new kings, as Manetho did when he was commissioned to write a history of Egypt, or lead a revolt against them, as Horwennefer did in 205 BCE.
tiers.why: Priests and other religious officials remained overwhelmingly Egyptian and kept much of their old privilege and prestige, because the Ptolemies relied on Egyptian religion to legitimise their rule.

tiers.name: Greek settlers
tiers.you: You came from Macedonia to serve the king, and he gave you thirty arouras in the Faiyum to farm in peacetime, with the duty to fight whenever he calls.
tiers.kid: Greek soldiers were given farms in Egypt, and in return they had to fight for the king whenever he called them.
tiers.rise: Greek immigrants, mercenaries and even prisoners of war entered by joining the army, and the cleruchs’ descendants, the epigonoi, kept their status. In time many people counted as Greeks were of Egyptian descent.
tiers.why: Macedonians and other Greeks were the kingdom’s privileged minority.

tiers.name: Egyptian soldiers
tiers.you: You are an Egyptian foot soldier holding five arouras of the king’s land, enough to feed your family, and your commanders sometimes send you to guard an official or help gather the taxes.
tiers.kid: Egyptian soldiers were given small farms too, and they helped the king’s army win a great battle at Raphia.
tiers.rise: An Egyptian entered the rank by enlisting. After Raphia, and under the reforms of Ptolemy V, native soldiers appeared more often as officers and cavalrymen, though Greeks kept the higher ranks of the royal guard, the officers’ posts and the generalships.
tiers.why: The machimoi were lower-ranking infantry, usually of Egyptian origin.

tiers.name: Jews and other immigrant communities
tiers.term: politeuma (a community of settlers of one origin)
tiers.you: Your family came from the southern Levant; you speak Greek rather than the Hebrew or Aramaic of your grandparents and live in the Jewish quarter of Alexandria.
tiers.kid: People came to Egypt from many lands, and Jewish families in Alexandria had their own part of the city.
tiers.rise: Many came as soldiers and were settled for their service: according to Josephus, Alexander the Great had settled Jews in Alexandria as a reward for military service. Their children grew up speaking Greek.
tiers.why: Of the many peoples who settled in Ptolemaic Egypt, the Greeks were the most privileged.

tiers.name: Peasant farmers
tiers.you: You farm a field whose produce belongs in part to the king, a temple or a noble family, and the officials of your nome take their share of every harvest; if you work for wages, you are paid in bronze.
tiers.kid: Most Egyptians were farmers who grew wheat beside the Nile and gave much of their harvest in taxes.
tiers.rise: A peasant’s son could enlist as a soldier and receive a small lot, or learn Greek and rise into the lower posts of the administration. Many Egyptians were moved from other parts of the country to new land in the Faiyum.
tiers.why: As before the Greeks came, peasant farmers were the vast majority of the people.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were seized in Syria and sold at Gaza to a new owner, who paid tax on your purchase; if you run away, he will offer a reward for your capture.
tiers.kid: Some people were enslaved, many of them brought from Syria and sold, and some tried to run away.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, on which the state took a tax. Running away was the other path, and the Ptolemaic period is the first from which documents of escape from slavery survive in any number.
tiers.why: Slavery in Ptolemaic Egypt was supplied by war, purchase, debt and, probably more rarely, birth.
